\label{sec:results}

% Overview
This section presents the outcomes of the bias detection and Talk page tone analyses, focusing on variation across topics and the relationship between participation diversity and neutrality.

\subsection{Talk Page Sentiment and Toxicity}
Sentiment analysis showed that discussions typically remained neutral, with only slight negative comments detected.

% Aggregate results (automatically generated)
The automated talk-page analysis produced per-topic summaries (counts and label distributions); the full machine-readable results are available in \path{paper/article_comparisons_results.json} and per-subset JSON files in the same directory. Representative comparison figures were saved to \path{figures/article\_comparisons\_default.png} (and other subset-specific PNGs).

Table~\ref{tab:talk-summary} summarizes the default subset (topics used in the main analysis). Percentages are relative to the number of comments extracted per talk page.
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\hline
Topic & \# Comments & Neutral (\%) & Negative (\%) \\
\hline
Donald Trump         & 14 & 92.9  & 7.1 \\
Antisemitism         & 2  & 100.0 & 0.0 \\
Capitalism           & 77 & 94.8  & 5.2 \\
Atheism              & 4  & 100.0 & 0.0 \\
British National Party & 3 & 100.0 & 0.0 \\
Feminism             & 4  & 100.0 & 0.0 \\
Gentrification       & 2  & 100.0 & 0.0 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Summary of Comments by Topic}
\label{tab:talk-summary}
\end{table}


These automated summaries show that the majority of extracted comments were labeled ``Neutral'' by the sentiment classifier, and toxicity scores were low for the sampled comments across topics. The saved figures (e.g., \texttt{figures/article\_comparisons\_default.png}) visualize the label distributions and confidence levels used to generate Table~\ref{tab:talk-summary}.

Notes and limitations: the counts reflect the subset of comments the script could extract (see the JSON files for exact counts), the sentiment model is a general-purpose classifier and may under- or over-count valenced language in politically charged discussions, and toxicity estimates are coarse (``Low/Medium/High'') based on classifier score thresholds. We treat these results as descriptive and exploratory; interpretation and causal claims are deferred to the Discussion.

\subsection{Subset summaries}
The analysis also produced subset-specific summaries (``political'', ``social'', and ``extremes'') whose JSON outputs are available as \path{paper/article\_comparisons\_results.political.json}, \path{paper/article\_comparisons\_results.social.json}, and \path{paper/article\_comparisons\_results.extremes.json}. In brief:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Political subset (Donald Trump, British National Party, Capitalism): distributions remain dominated by Neutral labels; Capitalism contributed the largest comment sample (77 comments) and therefore drives the aggregated counts.
	\item Social subset (Feminism, Gentrification, Atheism): small sample sizes (2--4 comments per topic) but similarly high proportions of Neutral labels in the extracted comments.
	\item Extremes subset (British National Party, Antisemitism): very small samples (2--3 comments per topic) and therefore highly variable; interpret cautiously.
\end{itemize}
